Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for the run-chase. The players head back to the middle. Rachin Ravindra and Devon Conway stride out to open the innings for New Zealand. It will be Matthew Forde to begin with the ball for the West Indies. Here we go!
…THE RUN CHASE…

Now, needing 248 for victory, New Zealand will need a composed batting effort, with at least one player stepping up for a big score to guide the team toward what would be an unassailable 2-0 lead. Will the home side chase it down, or will the West Indies bowlers rise to defend the total and level the series? We’ll find out soon. Stay tuned for the second essay.

Kiwi pacer, Nathan Smith, is down for a chat. He says that it was nice to get back into the game and get a few wickets. Adds that there was some movement but applauds Shai Hope and a few other batters, who punished them whenever they missed their lengths. Reckons that the total on board is gettable and hopes that he isn't needed and someone up the order gets a hundred.

For New Zealand, Nathan Smith was the standout bowler, claiming 4/42 in a crucial spell, while Kyle Jamieson made early inroads with three wickets. Mitchell Santner and Blair Tickner also contributed with one wicket each. However, Tickner and Henry were a bit expensive, conceding over 123 runs in their combined 13 overs. The West Indies capitalized on any loose deliveries and posted a strong total from a tricky position.

The innings, however, didn’t start smoothly for the Windies. Both Kyle Jamieson and Matt Henry bowled with precision, swinging the ball both ways, and reduced the visitors to a precarious 86/5 by the 16th over. It was then that Shai Hope anchored the innings, forging crucial partnerships with Justin Greaves, Matthew Forde, and Romario Shepherd. While the others rotated the strike, Hope remained steadfast at the crease, steadily guiding his team close to the 250-run mark.

An extraordinary and unbeaten knock of 109 off just 69 balls from West Indies captain Shai Hope has propelled his side to a formidable 247/9 in this shortened 34-over contest. The last nine overs alone yielded a staggering 111 runs, leaving the visitors in a commanding position as they headed into the dressing room.
A single to end the innings. Yorker length delivery on off. Shai Hope squeezes it toward the backward point region for a single. The West Indies finish with 247/9.

Commentary.Commentary: All in readiness now. The teams and the umpires make their way out to the ground. John Campbell and Ackeem Auguste stride out to open for the West Indies. It will be Matt Henry to begin with the ball for New Zealand. We are moments away from the live action.

Blair Tickner is up for a chat. He says the forecast has changed, so he’s hoping to get some gametime. He didn’t play the first game, so he’s fresh and ready to go. He mentions that the team has often been put in tough positions, but winning from there helps the group. Regarding the pitch, he notes that it’s usually dry, but with current conditions, some pace and bounce can be expected. He emphasizes the need to improve every time to consistently be in winning positions. The boundaries are smaller compared to those of Hagley Oval so planning will be crucial. He finishes by saying it’s great to be part of the group, playing alongside talented bowlers of different types, and he’s glad to be contributing.

Under the revised playing conditions, four bowlers will be allowed to bowl a maximum of seven overs each, while one bowler can bowl up to six overs. The first Powerplay will be during the initial seven overs.

West Indies skipper Shai Hope says they would have preferred to bowl first, but now the focus is on putting solid runs on the board. He adds that while the lower order has been contributing well, the top order needs to step up and deliver big scores. Hope shares that the team is confident, having played well in several close games. He emphasizes the importance of embracing the challenge and coming out on top. He also confirms one change in the lineup, with Ackeem Auguste replacing Alick Athanaze.

Mitchell Santner, the New Zealand skipper, wins the toss and elects to bowl. He says it’s always an advantage to know the target in these conditions. Santner adds that the West Indies possess a powerful lineup and are never out of the contest. He concludes by confirming that Daryl Mitchell misses out, with Mark Chapman coming into the XI.

New Zealand (Playing XI) - Devon Conway, Rachin Ravindra, Will Young, Mark Chapman (in for Daryl Mitchell), Tom Latham(WK), Michael Bracewell, Mitchell Santner(C), Nathan Smith (in for Zakary Foulkes), Kyle Jamieson, Matt Henry, Blair Tickner (in for Jacob Duffy).

West Indies (Playing XI) - John Campbell, Ackeem Auguste (in for Alick Athanaze), Keacy Carty, Shai Hope(C/WK), Sherfane Rutherford, Roston Chase, Justin Greaves, Romario Shepherd, Matthew Forde, Shamar Springer, Jayden Seales.
TOSS - New Zealand have won the toss and opted to BOWL.

UPDATE - 3.23 am GMT - Good news, everyone! The toss is scheduled for 3.30 am GMT, just under ten minutes from now, with play set to begin at 4.00 am GMT. It will be a 34-overs-per-side contest. Let’s hope the rain stays away.

UPDATE - 3.13 am GMT - The rain has eased to a light drizzle, and only the pitch remains under covers. The super soppers are making their rounds to dry the outfield. McLean Park is known for its excellent drainage, so once the rain stops, play shouldn’t take long to resume. The umpires are in discussion with the groundstaff, and there’s some movement suggesting the covers may soon come off. Let’s hope the weather holds from here.

UPDATE - 2.35 am GMT - The broadcast is back and scenes from Napier show a light but persistent drizzle, which is frustrating for everyone. We can also see a few of the players and even commentators chatting with an umbrella over their heads. According to a few sources, the cut-off time for the start of a 20-overs-a-side contest is 6.10 am GMT, which is still a long way away but if the rain keeps playing hide and seek like this, time will slip by quickly. Let's stay hopeful for now.

UPDATE - 2.12 am GMT - There is a ticker on the screen which shows that the toss will take place at 2.15 am GMT, which is in just a few minutes' time. This is very positive news and it seems like the umpires want to make the most of the dry conditions right away. Well, well! Just when the clock ticks over to 2.15 am GMT, the ticker shows that the 'toss is delayed,' which most likely means that the rain is back or at best the ground staff expect some rain pretty soon. The wait goes on...

UPDATE - 2.03 am GMT - The visuals from McLean Park show that the rain has once again stopped but it is still gloomy out there in the middle. The good news is that the umpires are now in the middle and they are having a chat with the ground staff. The previous spell of rain didn't have much ill effect on the conditions but the question now is whether we will get a sustained spell without any rain or not. Let's hope we do, and if that's the case, we should get some official news pretty soon, so stay tuned for more updates.

UPDATE - 1.34 am GMT - We have some more news coming in from the ground now. The toss was rescheduled for 2 am GMT and things looked positive for a while but the rain was back and we will once again have a delay. Also, the main pitch is currently under covers, but the rain seems to be fairly light right now. Let's hope we get a big chunk of the dry spell soon, so that we can get the play underway. Stick around for more updates.

UPDATE - 1 am GMT - Frankie Mackay, a fomer Whiter Ferns, later reports from pitchside that the covers are coming off and even though there's a bit more rain on the radar, the ground staff are hoping that it will skirt away from the venue and she adds that the surface in Napier has been resurfaced recently and it if one of the fastest drying grounds in the country.

UPDATE - 12.51 am GMT - Live visuals show grey skies and light rain still falling in the background. The ground staff are wiping off a bit of water off the outfield, not quite sure why but the on-air commentators mention that Napier is one of the driest parts of the country. A minute or so later, there's more activity near the main cover and we might just see the ground staff take the covers off here. Fingers crossed.

Not the news we would have wanted to hear but it's raining in Napier and for now, the toss has been delayed. There is forecast for more rain as well and all we can do is hope and wait for things to get better. Stay tuned for further updates.
So, will the Black Caps wrap up the series today, or can the West Indies stage a fightback to force a decider? We’ll find out soon. Toss and team news coming up. Stay tuned.

As for the West Indies, they were competitive throughout the first match but fell just short. Their bowlers did well to restrict New Zealand under 270, with Jayden Seales and Matthew Forde sharing five wickets and Roston Chase delivering a tidy spell. In the chase, several batters made promising starts but couldn’t convert, though Sherfane Rutherford scored a valuable 55 before falling at a crucial moment. Late cameos from Justin Greaves and Romario Shepherd kept hopes alive, but the Men in Maroon ultimately couldn’t cross the line. They will take heart from their performance and look to hit back strongly to keep the series alive.

In the first ODI, New Zealand posted 269/7 after being put in to bat. Daryl Mitchell was the star of the innings with a superb 119, supported well by Devon Conway, Michael Bracewell, and Zak Foulkes. With the ball, Kyle Jamieson led the attack with three wickets, while Matt Henry, Foulkes, and Mitchell Santner kept things tight to secure a narrow 7-run victory. The hosts, however, will be without Mitchell for this match due to injury, with Henry Nicholls replacing him. New Zealand will hope to replicate their all-round effort and seal the series.

Hello, and a warm welcome to our coverage of the second ODI of this three-match series from McLean Park in Napier. After edging out a thrilling win in the opening game, the Black Caps will be aiming to seal the series 2–0, while the West Indies will be desperate to bounce back and level things up.
... MATCH DAY ...

'Another chapter of tension awaits in this see-saw series!' After a gripping first ODI where New Zealand scraped home by just 7 runs, the stage is set for a fiery second encounter between the Kiwis and West Indies. The opener had everything - Daryl Mitchell’s composed hundred anchoring the hosts to a competitive total, Kyle Jamieson’s triple strike keeping New Zealand alive in the crunch moments, and a Windies chase full of promise but lacking that one big partnership. Most of the visiting batters got off to starts, yet only Sherfane Rutherford managed to convert, playing a blistering knock that kept the game alive until the final overs, with Justin Greaves and Sherfane Rutherford also fighting hard to take them close. For New Zealand, the batting still revolves around the stability of Rachin Ravindra, Devon Conway, and Tom Latham, while Will Young’s aggressive approach continues to give them momentum at the top. However, Mitchell has been ruled out for the remainder of this series due to a groin issue, which will be a big loss, but Michael Bracewell and Mitchell Santner's all-brilliance could well make up for it. Their bowling attack has clear strengths - Jamieson’s bounce, Matt Henry’s discipline, and Jacob Duffy’s knack of picking key wickets make them a dangerous unit, but death bowling remains a soft spot - something that nearly cost them the first game, and we saw that in the T20I series as well. As for West Indies, their power-packed lineup is never short of flair -  Shai Hope’s experience, Keacy Carty’s elegance, and Sherfane Rutherford’s return to form give them the ability to chase or set big totals, but their problem lies in inconsistency and the lack of someone to bat through the innings. With the ball, Matthew Forde and Jayden Seales have been impressive with swing and accuracy, and Roston Chase’s variations in the middle overs keep things tight, yet their inability to strike early or contain in the final overs continues to hurt them. With both sides showing glimpses of brilliance but not quite putting a complete performance together, the second ODI promises another nail-biter, and possibly a defining shift in momentum in this hard-fought series.
